title: Absalom, my son (2 Samuel 18:33)
hook: David's rebel son dies and the king weeps: would I had died for you

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nathan and the poor man's lamb. Your line was I have sinned against the Lord.

Two runners are coming across the plain. The king sits between the two gates of the city, waiting, and a watchman on the roof of the gate calls down what he sees. The battle is over, a battle against David's own son. Absalom, praised in all Israel for his looks, had stolen the people's hearts, declared himself king, and driven his father out of Jerusalem. Now the armies have met in a forest. The first runner arrives: the king's enemies are defeated. David asks only one question: is the young man Absalom safe?

Before the battle, David gave one order, in front of the whole army: "Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom." It wasn't obeyed. Absalom rode his mule under the thick branches of a great oak, his head caught fast, and he was left hanging between heaven and earth. Joab, the general, who had heard the king's order, thrust three darts into him, and Joab's armor-bearers finished it. A second runner comes. The runner says it gently: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is. David understands. In the King James Bible: "And the king was much moved, and went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept: and as he went, thus he said, O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!" Read it aloud and it barely holds together. It's a man climbing to a room over a gate, saying the same few words over and over. Some readers hear in it the shadow of Nathan's words: trouble rising from David's own house. None of that stops the grief. The text counts the cost too: the soldiers come back into the city quietly, like people ashamed, because their victory had turned into mourning. One Christian reading is a parent's love that outlasts betrayal and would trade places with the child who wronged him. Some Christians hear an echo of their teaching about Jesus: that God did what David could only wish, and died for those who had turned away.
screen: `WOULD GOD I HAD DIED FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Some of us know a mother or father who has lost a child, through death, or estrangement, or a road the child chose, and some of us are that parent; if someone comes to mind, let them come, gently. Don't try to say anything wise. If you pray, pray for them in silence or in your own words; if you don't, simply hold them with care.
Absalom. David's son, who rebelled against him and died in the forest, and whom the king mourned: would God I had died for thee.
Your line: my son, my son. Some grief is only a name, said again. Go gently.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to David's lament for Absalom when speaking of a parent's grief, and some hear in it a picture of God's love for those who have turned away.

chat.says: Absalom rebelled against David. So why did David weep so hard when he died?
options: He was still his son; David wished he had died in his place.
David was mostly upset that his army had disobeyed his order.
David feared Absalom's friends would now come to take revenge.
chat.meaning: Even after the rebellion, David grieved as a parent: O my son Absalom, would God I had died for thee.

Joab.meaning: David's general, who killed Absalom against the king's order

chamber over the gate.meaning: the room above the city gate, where David wept

Nathan.meaning: the prophet who warned of trouble from David's own house

notes: In Hebrew Bibles, 2 Samuel 18:33 is numbered 19:1; the script uses the English numbering.

Absalom praised for his looks (14:25), stealing the hearts (15:6), driving David out (15:14). The battle in the wood of Ephraim (18:6), the oak (18:9), Joab's darts (18:14); the script says only that Joab killed him.
'Is the young man Absalom safe?' paraphrases 18:29, 32; the Cushite's answer from 18:32. The soldiers 'as people being ashamed steal away' paraphrases 19:3.
The link to Nathan's words (12:10–11) is attributed to 'some readers'.
Closing line: 'in Christian teaching' God's love took the place of the one in the wrong (substitution). Confirm it is phrased fairly across Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox readers.
Pastoral sensitivity: the practice may touch listeners who have lost a child. Keeper to confirm tone.
